en.html:
...Ritsu did not come back.

Not home. Not to school. Not to us.

Now people were getting alarmed. Disappearances were not rare in Kanto these days, but what comfort was that supposed to give? It had happened to somebody we knew.

Suzukawa came to our classroom only that morning. Afterward, apparently, his rounds were Ritsu's house, the staff room, the police station. Several times I saw him striding down a corridor or across the schoolyard, his face stern.

A missing-person report must have been filed. But surely neither he nor the family expected that to settle anything. Same hope as dropping a coin in a shrine box.

Even a show of investigation would be better than usual. Probably one careless entry in some register, bas. Work finished.

In the past few years, not one story had reached me of the police protecting citizens. Big case, small case, nothing. Being used up by Rokuhara like subcontractors when anti-Shogunate people had to be rounded up—that, apparently, they did manage.

So relying on them, not even a little.

We would have to do it ourselves.

We reached the station.

The railway was Kanto's main transport artery. An ordinary citizen being allowed to make regular use of this artery—that was another matter. Once, things had been different.

Now it was practically the Shogunate's service train. Soldiers and military supplies, that was what it carried. A civilian could ride, certainly. First produce an unreasonable quantity of money.

For Edo or Sunpu, better take a boat. Slower, but cheap, with dependable sailings.

So Ritsu boarding a train here and going somewhere was hardly likely. That was not why we had come, anyway.

Only then did I notice.

Not the woman. That I had been hearing her playing all this while.

A large stringed instrument. She held it like a lover—or perhaps a child—and drew her bow across it.

Heavy, full, yet quiet. Like wind drifting deep inside a forest, where sunlight never reached.

A wind touching nobody. A sound reaching no ears.

Not one person stopped before her. The crowd flowed past, always hurrying.

They would not even remember hearing this music. Perhaps later, some unfamiliar melody would cross their minds, and they would wonder where it had come from.

Once I had noticed, I could hear how beautiful it was.
